releases.title: Share an app by link, straight from your Mac

sections.title: What's new
items: Share any app you own as a link. Open the app, click share, and choose copy link — or share…, which hands the link to the Mac share sheet so you can send it through Messages, Mail, Notes or AirDrop. The app is encrypted on your Mac before anything is uploaded; the link carries the key, and the relay stores bytes it cannot read.
You choose how long a link lasts — 24 hours, 1 week or 1 month — and can revoke it from the share sheet at any time.
Snug links open in the app: a snug:// link from a shared preview now lands on the same read-only preview inside Snug, where you can read the app's docs, try it, and install it.
A shared app's preview installs with one click. The separate keep step is gone.

sections.title: Good to know
items: What travels is the app's code, the shapes of its connections, its data structure and the docs you tick — never your data, your credentials or your approved connections.
A shared preview runs without your AI until you switch it on for that preview, so a stranger's app cannot spend your tokens on a click.

sections.title: What's new
items: The WhatsApp helper Telepath needs is now a one-click download inside the app — about 41 MB from GitHub, signed with the same key as Snug updates — offered the moment you open Telepath or start linking. No developer tools, no separate install.
The download is checked twice before anything runs: the signature, and a fingerprint this exact version of Snug was built with. Anything else is refused and nothing touches your disk.
If a linked WhatsApp session is on this computer but its helper is missing, a chip in the header says so instead of failing quietly.

The update sheet now shows only what changed since the version you are running — the notes for the release you already have no longer appear under the new one, and the sheet can no longer be cut off at the top of a small window.

sections.title: Good to know
items: The helper lives in ~/Snug/helpers and brings its own copy of Node, so nothing needs to be installed system-wide. It uses about 140 MB on disk once unpacked.
Installing the helper is always your click; Snug never downloads it on its own.

releases.title: You can always see which brain is thinking

sections.title: What's new
items: A brain chip in the header always names what is answering you — the demo brain, your own AI key, a local model, or the hub. It stays accurate as you switch.
Answers from the demo brain now carry a "scripted demo" tag on the turn itself, so canned output is never mistaken for a real model — including after you reopen the app.
Clicking the chip explains the current brain in one sentence and takes you straight to using your own key or a local model.
If a provider was selected but its key was missing, Snug used to quietly fall back to scripted answers with no signal. It now says so.

sections.title: Good to know
items: Your AI key is saved in your .snug file on this device and sent only to the provider you choose — never to Snug's servers.
The demo brain is a tiny offline script: no AI model, no server, no network.

sections.title: What's new
items: Snug for macOS — your apps, your data, one portable file, now in a native shell.
Native networking for connected apps: no browser CORS wall between you and your own providers.
Your .snug file lives in ~/Snug and opens with a double-click.
Optional passphrase protection for your file, with a Recovery Key that works when you forget.
Built-in update channel: the app tells you when a new version ships and shows you exactly what changed — installing is always your call.

sections.title: Good to know
items: macOS only through 1.0 — the Windows WebView cannot yet hold our app-sandbox promise, so we don't ship there.
Telepath's WhatsApp helper is a separate developer install and is not delivered by this download.
